summary_md: Simchon, Edwards and Lewandowsky (PNAS Nexus 2024, brief report) test whether matching a political ad's style to a reader's openness to experience raises perceived persuasiveness, and whether LLMs can mass-produce such matched ads. Four UK Prolific survey experiments (n = 440, 804, 803, 804) score each ad with a previously validated reader-side openness model and regress 1-5 perceived persuasion on person openness, ad openness and the mismatch |z(O_person) - z(O_ad)| in a mixed model with random intercepts for ads and participants. Mismatch lowers ratings with real Facebook ads (b = -0.07 and -0.08 per SD of mismatch) and with ChatGPT rewrites (b = -0.03, p < 0.001); GPT-3 rewrites miss significance (b = -0.01, p = 0.057). The authors call the effects small and convert them, by simulation on a midpoint cutoff, into 2,490 extra persuaded per 100,000 (median mismatch to none). The outcome is self-reported perceived persuasion, not attitude change or behaviour; only one trait is tested; reported t degrees of freedom do not square with the sample sizes, and study 2a/2b sample sizes are swapped between text and figure. For Paul's systems the paper is mostly a design contrast. Melange's receptivity layer treats Big Five traits as person-level main effects on susceptibility and seed probability, with no message-by-trait term, while this paper locates the effect in the interaction, above and beyond person openness. That is a modelling gap, not a recommendation: the population is the UK public rating ads, not legislators meeting lobbyists, the effects are small, and Melange's text-derived openness is its weakest trait. The paper's openness score also measures the appeal of text to open readers, a different construct from the author-trait openness Melange extracts from floor speech.

bearings.paper_claim: Persuasion depends on the fit between message style and recipient openness, above and beyond the recipient's own openness: mismatch coefficient b = -0.07 (study 1a, n = 440) and -0.08 (study 1b, n = 804) per SD of |z(O_person) - z(O_ad)| on a 1-5 perceived-persuasion scale, b = -0.03 for ChatGPT-tailored ads (n = 804), with person and ad openness held as separate predictors.
bearings.paper_location: Results, study 1 and study 2b, p.2-3; Fig. 1
bearings.system_side: The receptivity layer maps traits to person-level multipliers only: susc_trait = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E, susc_mult and edge_mult as affine gains of that one scalar, and on the lexical basis seed_prob = clip(0.60 + .10A + .06O + .04E, 0.30, 0.90). The default basis is behavioral (RECEPT_TRAITS defaults to behavioral), so lexical O does not enter seed_prob at all by default. No term varies with the content or framing of the ask; receptivity is message-invariant.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only if trait-message fit operates for legislators receiving lobbying asks as it does for UK Prolific adults rating Facebook ads; the outcome is self-reported perceived persuasion, not a vote or cosponsorship; effects are small (simulated 2,490 per 100,000 at a midpoint cutoff). Any matching term would need a message-side trait score Melange does not compute, and would stay UNVERIFIED until tested against the prospective H1/H2 contract.

bearings.paper_claim: The ad openness score comes from a language model trained to predict how attractive a text is to readers high in openness (Simchon et al. 2023, ref 13), not who wrote it; prompted ChatGPT rewrites shift that score by Cohen's d = 0.51 and GPT-3 rewrites by only d = 0.07, so the style can be produced on demand.
bearings.paper_location: Results, study 1 and study 2 validation, p.2
bearings.system_side: Melange scores author openness from floor speech and interview text with a closed-vocabulary linear map (O weights sixltr .30, insight .25, article .20, i -.15, certain -.10), refit to RKH targets. Held-out CV vs RKH for O is .214, the weakest of the five traits, and O is checked against an expected negative party sign.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows openness-styled text is easy to generate on demand (d = 0.51 with a simple prompt), which supports the worry that legislators' public text reflects staff and communications strategy rather than author trait; it does not validate author-side lexical O in either direction. Applies to Melange only as a construct-validity caution for O on prepared speech.

bearings.paper_claim: Personality-matched messaging produces small attitudinal increments (b = -0.03 to -0.08 per SD of mismatch on a 1-5 self-report), which the authors translate to 2,490 to 11,405 extra persuaded per 100,000 under a midpoint cutoff, with no behavioural outcome.
bearings.system_side: Untapped potential values persuasion as (1 - |2s - 1|) x t, a function of the voter's support position and turnout only; it is message-invariant and uses no personality data.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only relevant if Terrier ever tailors canvass scripts by inferred voter traits; the paper's effects are on perceived persuasion of ads in a UK online panel, not doorstep vote choice, so it does not argue for changing the potential formula.

gaps_exposed: No message-side model anywhere in the receptivity layer: susceptibility and seed probability are person-level only, so the system cannot represent the trait-by-message fit this paper identifies as the active ingredient.
Under the default behavioral basis, text-derived openness does not enter seed_prob, so any openness-based tailoring idea would have no live trait input to attach to.

Melange's author-side lexical openness (CV .214 vs RKH) is not distinguished from reader-appeal openness of text, a construct the paper's scoring model measures; prepared floor text may carry staff-crafted appeal style rather than member trait.
flags: Paper's own reporting inconsistencies: t degrees of freedom (26,348 for 440 participants x 9 ads; 48,173 for 804 x 10) exceed the rating counts implied by the samples, and study 2a/2b sample sizes are swapped between Methods and the Fig. 1 caption; quote the coefficients with this caveat.

Outcome is self-reported perceived persuasion; the 2,490 per 100,000 figure is a simulated extrapolation on a midpoint cutoff (window: 2023 fielding, UK Prolific adults; denominator: 100,000 simulated exposures), not observed persuasion.

Any matching term added to the receptivity layer would be new analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062); it would also be a rank-moving recalibration that is Paul's call.
No conflict with the barred SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025: the paper makes no network, edge-weight or LDA claims.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated-bibliography entry and no markup for this work (0 annotations), so there is no takeaway of his to test. His receptivity-layer position (traits adjust response to pressure) treats traits as person-level modifiers, as the code does. This paper qualifies that: its trait effect lives in message-recipient fit. It does not justify a matching term: public ad ratings, small effects, and Melange's weakest trait (O).

related.why: Cited as ref 10 for microtargeting working even on a single attribute; Tappin measures persuasive returns to targeting with real attitude outcomes, a stronger test than this paper's perceived-persuasion ratings.
A systematic review of personality as a moderator of persuasion strategies; it places this paper's openness-matching result within the wider trait-by-message literature.
An agent-based model of why microtargeted campaigning pays at scale; it is the theoretical counterpart to this paper's argument that small per-person effects add up across 100,000 exposures.
Byrne supplies the person-level trait-to-susceptibility composite in Melange's receptivity layer; Simchon shows a message-by-trait interaction that a main-effects composite cannot capture.
A meta-analysis of inferring Big Five traits from digital footprints, the inference step this paper's manipulation machine assumes on the recipient side.
A meta-analysis of LIWC and Big Five links that bounds how much openness signal closed-vocabulary text carries, relevant to both this paper's text scoring and Melange's lexical O.
